# Wirecard / Jan Marsalek Public-Fraud Trail

## Executive summary

The benchmark evidence supports only a partial reconstruction of the Wirecard public-fraud trail.

The available evidence consists of two sources:

- A Wirecard corporate disclosure dated 28 April 2020 concerning the KPMG special investigation (`SRC-001`).
- A November 2020 Economic Governance Support Unit study requested by the European Parliament’s ECON Committee (`SRC-002`).

Together, these sources establish the following:

1. Wirecard publicly represented in April 2020 that KPMG had found no incriminating evidence of alleged balance-sheet forgery and no significant findings requiring adjustments to the 2016–2018 annual accounts.
2. The same disclosure contained important limitations: KPMG could not obtain all data it considered necessary to prove certain revenues because the data were primarily controlled by third parties.
3. Wirecard also reported documentation and organizational weaknesses and announced that its annual accounts and annual press conference would be delayed.
4. A later institutional policy study assessed that multiple lines of defense—including internal controls, the supervisory board, external audit, financial-reporting oversight, and BaFin—had failed “in one way or another.” That assessment was expressly presented as the authors’ opinion, not necessarily the official position of the European Parliament or BaFin.
5. The benchmark evidence does not contain a source establishing the alleged missing €1.9 billion, trustee-account problems, the final EY audit opinion, official BaFin or ESMA findings, prosecutorial findings, or Jan Marsalek’s disappearance and alleged external connections.

Accordingly, the evidence supports a documented contrast between Wirecard’s April 2020 public representations and a later institutional assessment of systemic oversight failure. It does **not** support a complete factual reconstruction of the missing-cash episode or Marsalek’s disappearance.

## Evidentiary scope and limits

Only two unique source IDs were returned by the benchmark tools:

- `SRC-001`: [Wirecard AG: KPMG delivers report on special investigation](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation)
- `SRC-002`: [What are the wider supervisory implications of the Wirecard case?](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf)

No entity IDs, relationship IDs, or formally named relationships were returned by the tools. Consequently, no such identifiers are used below.

The searches sought additional evidence concerning:

- the alleged missing €1.9 billion;
- trustee accounts;
- June 2020 Wirecard disclosures;
- EY’s final audit opinion;
- BaFin, ESMA, governmental, parliamentary, and prosecutorial findings;
- Jan Marsalek’s disappearance;
- alleged intelligence or political connections.

Those searches returned no additional source IDs or source excerpts. These subjects are therefore treated as unsupported or unresolved rather than incorporated as established facts.

## 1. Wirecard’s public statements and representations

### 1.1 The 28 April 2020 KPMG disclosure

Wirecard issued an inside-information announcement under Article 17 of the Market Abuse Regulation on 28 April 2020. The announcement stated that Wirecard had received the KPMG special-audit report and that the report would be published on the company’s transparency website. [Wirecard AG: KPMG delivers report on special investigation](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation) (`SRC-001`)

The central public representation was:

> “Incriminating evidence for the public allegations of balance sheet forgery has not been identified.”

Wirecard also stated that, across the areas examined—Third Party Acquiring, Merchant Cash Advance/Digital Lending, and business activities in India and Singapore—KPMG had made:

> “no significant findings, which would require an adjustment of the annual accounts 2016-2018.”

These statements establish what Wirecard told the market. They do not independently prove that the representations were accurate, nor do they constitute a direct excerpt from the KPMG report in the available benchmark evidence.

### 1.2 Representation about revenue evidence

Wirecard stated that, during the audits of the 2016–2018 annual accounts:

> “the available documents and audit measures were sufficient for the proof of the revenues in the Third Party Acquiring business.”

This was a company representation about the sufficiency of audit evidence for TPA revenues. The available source does not independently verify the underlying documents, the audit procedures, or the accuracy of the conclusion.

### 1.3 The company’s express caveat about missing data

The same announcement contained a significant qualification:

> “not all data could be obtained that would have been required to proof the revenues in these years, because the required data are primarily in the control of third parties.”

This caveat matters because it qualifies the apparently reassuring statement that available documents and audit measures were sufficient. It shows that, according to Wirecard’s own account, KPMG’s heightened forensic requirements could not be fully met with all potentially relevant data.

The source does not specify:

- which precise data were unavailable;
- which transactions or counterparties were affected;
- whether the limitation prevented a conclusion;
- whether the limitation concerned all TPA revenue or only particular periods;
- how KPMG assessed the reliability of alternative evidence.

Those points remain unresolved.

### 1.4 December 2019 data

Wirecard stated that it controlled the necessary data for December 2019 and had provided:

> “more than 200 mio data relating to December 2019 sets”

to KPMG for forensic examination.

Wirecard further stated:

> “This audit has not revealed any deviations between the reported revenues and account balances.”

This was a company-reported result concerning December 2019 data. The available evidence does not establish whether this exercise resolved the earlier data limitations concerning 2016–2018, nor whether it addressed other elements of the business.

### 1.5 Documentation and organizational weaknesses

Wirecard reported that KPMG had identified:

> “documentation and organizational weaknesses during the audit period”

and said that these weaknesses had already been identified by Wirecard.

The company stated that it was addressing them through:

> “establishing a Global Compliance Organization and with the support of external consultants.”

The evidence supports the existence of this reported disclosure. It does not establish:

- the precise nature or severity of the weaknesses;
- whether they affected financial reporting;
- whether they contributed to any alleged misstatement;
- whether the remedial measures were effective or complete.

### 1.6 Delay to annual accounts and annual press conference

Wirecard announced that:

> “The release of the annual accounts and the annual press conference will not take place on 30 April 2020.”

It said that it would coordinate with auditor E&Y concerning when audit procedures could be completed, taking account of COVID-related restrictions and the completion of the KPMG report.

This establishes a delay and a stated intention to coordinate with EY. The benchmark evidence does not contain the subsequent EY opinion or the eventual result of that coordination.

## 2. Audit findings, limitations, and uncertainty

### 2.1 What the evidence says about KPMG

The available source does not provide the KPMG report itself. Instead, it provides Wirecard’s account of that report.

The company’s reported characterization was:

- no identified incriminating evidence for public allegations of balance-sheet forgery;
- no significant findings requiring adjustments to the 2016–2018 accounts;
- no deviations between reported revenues and account balances in the examined December 2019 data;
- documentation and organizational weaknesses during the audit period;
- inability to obtain all data required under KPMG’s increased forensic requirements.

These points must therefore be separated into two categories:

**Directly supported as company statements**

- Wirecard made the representations described above.
- Wirecard disclosed the data limitation and organizational weaknesses.
- Wirecard announced the delay to its annual accounts and press conference.

**Not independently established by the available evidence**

- That KPMG’s conclusions were accurately summarized by Wirecard.
- That the absence of reported findings meant the accounts were accurate.
- That the December 2019 data were complete or reliable.
- That the disclosed weaknesses were immaterial.
- That the data limitation had no impact on the reliability of earlier revenue figures.

### 2.2 No final EY opinion in the benchmark evidence

The benchmark extracts do not contain an EY audit opinion, qualification, disclaimer, adverse conclusion, or statement of inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence.

It is therefore not possible, using only the returned evidence, to state:

- what EY concluded;
- whether EY qualified the accounts;
- whether EY refused or was unable to sign an opinion;
- what specific audit evidence EY obtained or lacked;
- how EY’s position related to KPMG’s special investigation.

Any such conclusion would exceed the evidence returned by the tools.

### 2.3 The significance of the data limitation

The disclosure creates an evidentiary tension:

- Wirecard said the available documents and audit measures were sufficient to prove TPA revenues.
- Wirecard also said KPMG could not obtain all data that would have been required under increased forensic requirements because the data were controlled by third parties.

The available evidence does not determine whether these statements are formally contradictory. They may refer to different evidentiary standards:

- the evidence considered sufficient in the ordinary annual-account audits; and
- the additional evidence sought under a heightened forensic investigation.

However, the source does not explain the distinction in enough detail to resolve the issue. The proper conclusion is that the disclosure contains both a positive representation about sufficiency and a material caveat about unavailable third-party data.

## 3. Missing cash, trustee accounts, and alleged €1.9 billion

### 3.1 What is supported

The returned evidence supports only the following money- and documentation-related points:

- Wirecard referred to TPA revenues.
- Wirecard stated that some data were controlled by third parties.
- Wirecard reported documentation and organizational weaknesses.
- Wirecard referred to reported revenues and account balances for December 2019 data.

### 3.2 What is not supported

Neither returned source mentions:

- €1.9 billion;
- missing cash;
- trustee accounts;
- a specific trustee;
- a specific bank;
- bank confirmations;
- the location or status of funds;
- forged, missing, or unreliable account confirmations;
- a specific transfer of money;
- the June 2020 cash disclosure.

The alleged missing-cash and trustee-account episode therefore cannot be reconstructed from the benchmark evidence. It must be marked as **unsupported within the returned source set**, rather than presented as a verified event.

### 3.3 Consequence for the overall trail

The evidence does not establish a causal chain from:

1. Wirecard’s April 2020 statements;
2. the KPMG data limitation;
3. an alleged trustee-account failure;
4. missing cash; and
5. a particular later event.

Such a chain may be part of the broader public history of the Wirecard case, but it is not established by the sources returned here. The report therefore cannot attribute the alleged missing cash to any particular person, account, institution, audit failure, or corporate statement.

## 4. Regulatory, supervisory, governmental, and institutional assessments

### 4.1 The Economic Governance Support Unit study

`SRC-002` is a study titled *What are the wider supervisory implications of the Wirecard case?* It was prepared for the European Parliament’s Committee on Economic and Monetary Affairs by the Economic Governance Support Unit.

The study stated that:

> “all lines of defense against corporate fraud, including internal control systems, external audits, the oversight bodies for financial reporting and auditing and the market supervisor, contributed to the scandal and are in need of reform.”

The study identified five lines of defense and stated:

> “all five lines of defence against corporate fraud and deception have failed in one way or another.”

The five categories identified in the study were:

1. the company’s internal control system;
2. the supervisory board;
3. external audit;
4. oversight bodies for financial reporting and auditing;
5. the market supervisor, identified in the passage as BaFin.

The study further described the root cause, in the authors’ view, as:

> “a flawed market and institutional oversight architecture”

and stated that the existing system was:

> “not sufficiently fit to preserve market integrity and investor protection.”

These are institutional and policy assessments by the study’s authors. They are not, on the available evidence, judicial findings or final determinations of legal liability.

### 4.2 Status and qualification of the study

The study contains important caveats:

- It was requested by the European Parliament’s ECON Committee.
- It was prepared by named academic authors.
- It states that the opinions expressed are the sole responsibility of the authors.
- It states that those opinions do not necessarily represent the official position of the European Parliament.
- A footnote states that one author’s opinions were entirely personal and did not reflect a position taken by BaFin.

Accordingly, the study can be used as evidence that these authors assessed the oversight architecture as defective. It cannot be used, without further evidence, to establish that:

- the European Parliament officially adopted every conclusion;
- BaFin accepted the assessment;
- every named institution committed a legally actionable failure;
- a particular individual caused the Wirecard events;
- the study itself proved the underlying accounting allegations.

### 4.3 Information flows and oversight weaknesses

The study’s contents identify several areas of concern:

- blocked information flows;
- weaknesses in external audits;
- weaknesses in internal oversight;
- weaknesses in market forces;
- impaired enforcement of financial-information disclosure;
- the overarching mandate and accountability of the market supervisor.

The available excerpt establishes that these topics were addressed by the study. It does not provide the full factual analysis underlying every section. Consequently, detailed claims about specific regulatory decisions, warnings, complaints, or institutional communications are not supported by the returned excerpts.

### 4.4 Recommendations rather than established events

The study recommended reforms including:

- stronger accountability for external auditors;
- improved information flows to markets and supervisors;
- stronger internal-control requirements for listed companies;
- consideration of internal-control audits;
- stronger supervisory and enforcement powers for BaFin;
- forensic and investigative tools for BaFin;
- a reduced role for self-regulatory enforcement bodies such as FREP.

These are recommendations. The returned evidence does not establish that any particular recommendation was enacted, accepted, or implemented.

### 4.5 Institutions named in the study

The study includes abbreviations and references to bodies and regulatory concepts including BaFin, ESMA, APAS, FREP, national competent authorities, the European Commission, and other European and national institutions.

However, the mere appearance of an institution in the study’s abbreviations or comparative framework does not establish that it took a particular action in the Wirecard matter. No specific official action by BaFin, ESMA, a parliamentary inquiry, a prosecutor, or a governmental body is supported by the returned excerpts beyond the general policy discussion in `SRC-002`.

## 5. Jan Marsalek’s disappearance and alleged connections

### 5.1 No source-supported account of the disappearance

Neither `SRC-001` nor `SRC-002` mentions Jan Marsalek.

The benchmark evidence therefore does not establish:

- that Marsalek disappeared;
- the date or location of any disappearance;
- whether an arrest warrant was issued;
- whether he was investigated or charged;
- where he went;
- whether he had connections to intelligence services, political actors, governments, or criminal organizations;
- whether his disappearance was caused by or connected to Wirecard’s financial problems.

These matters must remain explicitly unresolved in an evidence-bounded report.

### 5.2 No supported connection to the corporate or supervisory trail

Because no returned source mentions Marsalek, the evidence does not support a relationship between him and:

- the KPMG special investigation;
- the unavailable third-party data;
- Wirecard’s documentation weaknesses;
- the alleged missing cash;
- trustee accounts;
- BaFin or other regulators;
- the institutional failures described in `SRC-002`.

Any such connection would require additional source evidence and cannot be inferred from the two returned sources.

## 6. Evidence-based reconstruction of the trail

The strongest reconstruction supported by the benchmark evidence is as follows:

1. **Wirecard faced public allegations concerning its accounts.**  
   This is reflected in Wirecard’s own April 2020 announcement, which referred to public allegations of balance-sheet forgery. [SRC-001]

2. **Wirecard publicly presented the KPMG investigation as not having identified incriminating evidence or adjustments to the 2016–2018 accounts.**  
   These were company representations about the special investigation. [SRC-001]

3. **The same disclosure acknowledged material evidentiary limitations.**  
   Wirecard stated that not all data required under KPMG’s increased forensic requirements could be obtained because relevant data were primarily controlled by third parties. [SRC-001]

4. **Wirecard also disclosed organizational and documentation weaknesses.**  
   It said that KPMG had identified such weaknesses and that Wirecard was undertaking remediation. [SRC-001]

5. **The annual-accounting timetable was delayed.**  
   Wirecard postponed the annual accounts and press conference and stated that it would coordinate with EY. [SRC-001]

6. **A later policy study assessed the broader oversight architecture as defective.**  
   The study attributed failures, in one way or another, to internal controls, the supervisory board, external audit, reporting and audit oversight, and market supervision. [SRC-002]

7. **The evidence does not bridge the remaining gaps.**  
   It does not establish the alleged €1.9 billion shortfall, trustee-account issues, the final EY position, official regulatory findings, or Jan Marsalek’s disappearance and alleged connections.

The result is not a complete chronology of the Wirecard scandal. It is a limited, source-bounded trail showing how a company’s reassuring public representation coexisted with acknowledged forensic-data limitations and a later institutional assessment of systemic oversight weakness.

## 7. Contradictions, tensions, and unresolved questions

### 7.1 Company reassurance versus institutional criticism

Wirecard stated that no incriminating evidence of balance-sheet forgery had been identified and that no significant findings required adjustments to the 2016–2018 accounts. [SRC-001]

The later study stated that all five lines of defense against corporate fraud and deception had failed in some way and that the oversight architecture was not sufficiently fit to protect market integrity and investors. [SRC-002]

These statements are in tension but are not directly equivalent:

- `SRC-001` records Wirecard’s contemporaneous account of KPMG’s findings.
- `SRC-002` provides a broader policy assessment of institutional oversight.

Neither source, in the available excerpts, definitively resolves the truth of the company’s representations or establishes the legal responsibility of any institution.

### 7.2 Sufficiency of available evidence versus unavailable forensic data

Wirecard said that the available documents and audit measures were sufficient to prove TPA revenues. It also said that not all data required under KPMG’s increased forensic requirements could be obtained. [SRC-001]

This may reflect different audit standards or scopes, but the source does not explain the distinction sufficiently to determine whether the statements are substantively inconsistent. The unresolved issue is whether the unavailable third-party data materially affected the reliability of the revenue evidence.

### 7.3 No source-supported contradiction concerning missing cash or Marsalek

No contradiction can be identified concerning:

- the alleged missing €1.9 billion;
- trustee accounts;
- Jan Marsalek;
- his disappearance;
- alleged intelligence or political links.

The reason is not that those matters are disproven, but that they are absent from the returned benchmark evidence.

## 8. Overall conclusion

The benchmark evidence supports a cautious reconstruction rather than a complete public-fraud narrative.

The documented trail begins with Wirecard’s April 2020 public account of the KPMG investigation. Wirecard presented the investigation as having found no incriminating evidence of balance-sheet forgery and no significant findings requiring changes to the 2016–2018 accounts. At the same time, the company disclosed that KPMG could not obtain all data it considered necessary under increased forensic requirements, because relevant information was controlled by third parties. Wirecard also acknowledged documentation and organizational weaknesses and delayed its annual-accounting timetable.

A later European Parliament-commissioned policy study assessed the case as exposing weaknesses across multiple layers of corporate and market oversight. That assessment is significant, but it remains an authors’ institutional-policy analysis rather than a judicial or independently verified finding of liability.

The benchmark evidence does not support the central missing-cash and trustee-account allegations, does not provide the final EY audit position, and does not contain evidence about Jan Marsalek’s disappearance or alleged broader connections. Those issues must therefore remain explicitly unresolved rather than being linked through inference.
